l: people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The people welcome Tang’s progress like rain in drought, continue markets and field work, and later receive King Wu’s tranquillity, gifts, and allegiance to Zhou.

l: king Wu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: King Wu, sovereign of Zhou, proceeds against those rejecting Zhou, punishes Shang, and gives tranquillity to their people by rescuing them from fire and water and seizing and destroying oppressors.

l: Wu's campaign against Shang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Wu invades Shang to seize oppressors; people welcome him with gifts and become Zhou subjects, a campaign compared to Tang’s justice.

l: Shang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: has oppressors [whose seizure is the campaign's purpose] Some people of Shang would not become subjects of Zhou until king Wu proceeded against them. After Wu’s campaign, Shang’s people were given tranquillity and welcomed him, while Shang’s oppressors were seized and destroyed.

l: oppressors, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The oppressors of Shang were seized and destroyed by Wu. His campaign is described as saving the people from the midst of fire and water while targeting only those oppressors.

l: Dai Bu Sheng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: desires king of Song [to be virtuous] Dai Bu Sheng is told by Mencius how the king of Song may be made virtuous. He agrees that a great officer of Chu would employ a man of Qi to teach his son the speech of Qi.

l: king of Song, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The king of Song is placed in attendance with Xue Ju Zhou, whom Dai Bu Sheng supposes to be a scholar of virtue. Mencius says that one Xue Ju Zhou cannot accomplish much alone for the king.

l: Xue Ju Zhou, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Xue Ju Zhou, a scholar of virtue attending the king of Song, exemplifies attendants whose shared virtue would leave the king no partners in evil.

l: attendants on the king, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The attendants on the king include people of varied ages and status. Their character determines whether the king has companions for good or evil: all Xue Ju Zhous prevent evil, while none prevent good.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Virtue is associated with Xue Ju Zhou, who is supposed to be a scholar of virtue. Mencius explains that the king’s exposure to virtuous or non-virtuous attendants affects what the king can do.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius what point of righteousness is involved in not going to see the princes.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_involved_in not going to see the princes Righteousness is discussed in relation to whether one should go to see princes and how one maintains proper conduct toward them.

l: not going to see the princes, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Not going to see the princes is examined through examples of avoidance, including Duan Gan Mu and Xie Liu, whose scrupulosity Mencius considers excessive.

l: Yang Huo, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Yang Huo wants Confucius to visit, but Confucius dislikes his improper approach of sending a roasted pig while he is away.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: nourishes spirit which the superior man nourishes The superior man is described through the spirit he nourishes, which can be understood by considering the remarks of Zengzi and Zi Lu.

l: spirit which the superior man nourishes, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_nourished_by superior man The spirit which the superior man nourishes is identified as something revealed by remarks condemning flattering behavior and insincere dealings.

l: Dai Ying Zhi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Dai Ying Zhi cannot immediately abolish duties or levy only a tithe, proposing temporary tax and duty reductions until ending them next year.

l: tithe, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a levy [a tithe] The levying of a tithe is presented as a measure Dai Ying Zhi is not able to implement immediately.

l: duties, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Duties at passes and markets are lightened until next year, then abolished under Dai Ying Zhi’s proposal.

l: tax, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Dai Ying Zhi proposes to lighten the tax until next year and then make an end of it.

l: man who appropriates fowls, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: A man habitually takes his neighbor’s stray fowls daily; challenged, he proposes reducing to one monthly until next year before stopping.

l: strayed fowls, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The strayed fowls belong to the man’s neighbor and are appropriated by the man in Mencius’s example.

l: appropriation of fowls, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a unrighteousness The appropriation of the neighbor’s strayed fowls is described as a practice that should be ended immediately once its unrighteousness is recognized.

l: unrighteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: should_be_ended immediately [with all despatch] Mencius says that if a person knows something is unrighteous, he should use all despatch to put an end to it rather than wait until next year.

l: the great inundation, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The great inundation drove waters wildly through the country and people into nests, platforms, or caves; Yu opened channels, conducted waters to the sea, and reduced it to order.

l: the principles that mark sages, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: fall_into_decay decay [after the death of Yao and Shun] The principles that mark sages fell into decay after the deaths of Yao and Shun. Their decline accompanied the rise of oppressive sovereigns and disorder.

l: the Spring and Autumn, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The Spring and Autumn, completed by Confucius during disorder, contains matters proper to the sovereign and prompts knowledge and condemnation of him.

l: Yang Zhu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: has_words_that_fill the country [alongside Mo Di's words] Yang Zhu's words filled the country alongside those of Mo Di. Mencius opposes Yang Zhu's doctrine because it does not acknowledge the claims of the sovereign.

l: Yang's principle, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Yang's principle holds each one for himself and does not acknowledge the claims of the sovereign.

l: Mo's principle, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mo's principle is loving all equally, but Mencius says it denies the special affection owed to a father.

l: the doctrines of the former sages, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mencius addresses himself to defending the doctrines of the former sages and opposing Yang and Mo. He says that sages who rise again will not change his words.

l: father-deniers and king-deniers, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: are_smitten_by Zhou Gong [according to Mencius's wish] Father-deniers and king-deniers are associated with the doctrines of Mo and Yang, which reject the special affection due to a father or the claims of the sovereign. Mencius says that Zhou Gong would have smitten them.

l: the three sages, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The three sages controlled waters, restored order, and completed the Spring and Autumn; Mencius seeks to continue their work.

l: Kuang Zhang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Kuang Zhang presents Chen Zhong as a man of true self-denying purity. He points to Chen Zhong's hunger in Wu Ling and his eating of worm-eaten plums as evidence.

l: Chen Zhong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Chen Zhong, of Qi's ancient noble family, lives in Wu Ling, makes hemp sandals, and eats millet. He refuses Dai's unrighteous emolument and house, enduring starvation until worm-eaten plums revive him. Yet his self-denying purity is questioned because he accepts goose flesh from his wife and still dwells in Wu Ling.

l: Wu Ling, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Wu Ling is where Chen Zhong lived after avoiding his brother and leaving his mother. Chen Zhong later returned to his family's house for a time.

l: self-denying purity, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Self-denying purity is the quality Kuang Zhang attributes to Chen Zhong. Mencius says Chen Zhong does not truly possess it because his conduct is inconsistent.

l: earthworm, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: A creature eats dry mould above and drinks the yellow spring below; Mencius says becoming it would fulfill Chen Zhong’s principles.

l: Dai, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Dai, Chen Zhong's elder brother, receives 10,000 zhong from Gai, whose emolument and house Chen Zhong rejects as unrighteous.

l: principles held by Chen Zhong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: require_becoming earthworm [to be carried out] The principles held by Chen Zhong require rejecting property and food considered unrighteous. Mencius says they could only be consistently carried out by an earthworm and points to Chen Zhong's acceptance of his wife's food as an inconsistency.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: This document is Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part I with a brief overview of Part II. It presents Mencius’s teaching that effective rule and personal conduct rest on benevolence, righteousness, propriety, sincerity, self-examination, and the models of ancient sages. He argues that skill and good intentions require laws, instruments, and the practices of the ancient kings; disorder arises when rulers and ministers ignore principle and propriety. States ultimately depend on the person of their heads, families depend on their heads, and kingdoms depend on States. Benevolence wins and preserves thrones by gaining the people’s hearts, whereas oppressive rulers such as Jie and Zhou lose them and drive people toward Tang and Wu. Rulers should imitate Yao, ministers Shun, and princes king Wen; a ruler corrected in mind will make his acts and kingdom correct as well. Mencius repeatedly turns responsibility inward: when love, government, or courtesy fails to receive a response, one should examine oneself. Self-caused disgrace and calamity are especially destructive, while sincerity, grounded in knowing the good, enables a person to move others. The work also treats practical duty: love parents, respect elders, preserve oneself in order to serve parents, and distinguish true filial piety from merely feeding parents. Shun’s devotion to Gu Sou exemplifies great filial piety. Mencius condemns ministers who enrich rulers through oppressive exactions and war, as well as people who reject benevolence and righteousness, pursue food and drink, or seek riches, honours, gain, and advancement deceptively. Dialogues with Chun Yu Kun, Gong Sun Chou, Yue Zheng, and others clarify that principles, not expedients, rescue a kingdom; fathers should avoid teaching sons when it creates alienation; and character may be discerned through words and the pupil of the eye. Part II continues these concerns through teachings on sages, rulers, ministers, scholars, learning, steadfast conduct, and exemplary behavior.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Mencius is a speaker and teacher who presents a connected teaching on government, conduct, and personal responsibility. He holds that virtue alone does not suffice for government: laws must be properly implemented, high stations belong to the benevolent, and rulers must be urged toward difficult achievements, good conduct, and the removal of perversity. Benevolence is the central condition of rule, enabling dynasties to gain the throne and preserving rulers, States, and the kingdom through gaining the people and their hearts. Righteousness, propriety, sincerity, respect, economy, and right principles also guide both rulers and individuals. The teaching moves from models supplied by sages and rulers such as Yao, Shun, king Wen, Bo Yi, and Tai Gong to practical accounts of ministers, princes, families, and the people. It insists that failure in love, government, or politeness calls for inward examination; that character is revealed by words and the pupil of the eye; and that people must follow duties that are near and easy, including loving parents and respecting elders. Mencius also addresses exceptions to ordinary rules, the proper education of sons, service to parents, rectifying a sovereign's mind, praise and reproach, and the evils of teaching others merely for self-interest. It closes by gathering benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, propriety, and music most fully into service to parents and obedience to elder brothers, while extending these principles to rulers, ministers, and public life.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Yao, an ancient king, rules as a model sovereign whose conduct should be imitated from beginning to end.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Shun is an ancient king, born in Zhu Feng, removed to Fu Xia, and dying in Ming Tiao. He serves Yao with exemplary respect and is presented as a model for ministers. He marries without telling his parents, fearing no posterity, an act superior men regard as equivalent to informing them. Though the kingdom joyfully submits to him, he values it little beside gaining his parents’ hearts and complete accord with them. He fully serves Gu Sou until Gu Sou delights in good, carries sage principles into practice in the Middle Kingdom, and is the same as other men.

l: princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Princes may have benevolent hearts and a reputation for benevolence, yet give people no benefits or future ages no example if they do not practice ancient kings’ ways. Though lacking benevolence, they treat perils as safety and calamities as profitable, delighting in what destroys States and ruins Families.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The people receive no benefit from benevolent intentions unless ancient ways are practiced, and suffer when oppression and wickedness come from high stations. Their hearts are central: gaining them requires collecting what they like and avoiding what they dislike, and they turn to benevolent rule as water flows downward. They may be injured by extreme oppression, governed unsuccessfully by inferiors lacking sovereign confidence, burdened with doubled grain payments and forced cultivation, or despised and plundered by fearful princes. Respectful and economical rulers neither despise nor plunder them.

l: ancient kings, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Ancient kings established governmental ways and laws, whose observance is presented as preventing error.

l: sages, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The sages use instruments to shape and tune things, then perfectly exhibit human relations.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The kingdom is a political whole rooted in the State and shaped by the conduct of rulers, princes, people, and families. Walls, weapons, land, and wealth do not make it safe; righteousness, law, propriety, and learning matter more. Violations by superiors and inferiors bring calamity, while extreme oppression causes it to perish and lesser oppression weakens it. It is gained by gaining the people: a benevolent ruler or prince attracts submission, faces no opponent, and may give laws to the kingdom. The kingdom can be ruined if not improved and is portrayed as drowning, requiring rescue through right principles. Its transformation culminates when people submit with delight, Gu Sou finds delight in what is good, and fathers and sons are established in their respective duties.

l: State, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A State has the family as its root and affects those affected by great families. Without principled rulers, lawful ministers, propriety, and learning, it survives only by chance and perishes quickly when seditious people spring up.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The Book of Poetry contains ancient statutes and teachings cited in Mencius. It urges fidelity to old rules, vigilance as Heaven produces Zhou’s overthrow, remembrance that Yin’s beacon is near in the last sovereign of Xia, and studious harmony with God’s ordinances. It moves from warning against transgression and ease toward happiness through diligence, while cautioning that otherwise the kingdom goes to ruin.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Heaven has God’s ordinances, governs a kingdom, and may produce the overthrow of Zhou. Harmony with its ordinances brings much happiness; it establishes political submission under both right and bad government, preserves those who accord with it, and causes rebels to perish. It sends escapable calamities, receives sacrifice from a wicked man after reform, and is associated with sincerity, the way of Heaven.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Benevolent government arises from concern for human suffering and is necessary to secure tranquil order in the kingdom. It lets benevolence overspread the kingdom and attracts people as water flows downward. Though a standard for princes, it may go unpractised; ministers enriching a prince without it are rejected by Confucius.

l: government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Government requires both virtue and laws, follows the ways of former kings when wise, and is guided by concern for men’s sufferings. If ruling others fails, the ruler should examine his own wisdom.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Benevolence is the tranquil habitation of man and a practice of loving and nourishing others through excellence. It matters most in government: when a benevolent person occupies high station, it benefits those below, overspreads the kingdom, gains the people, removes opponents, and supports the flourishing and preservation of States. Without it, rulers cannot preserve what they hold and face sorrow, disgrace, death, and ruin. A prince’s benevolence makes all his acts benevolent, while violating it leads toward perishing and makes productive discussion impossible. Benevolence also directs personal conduct: one should examine oneself when love is not returned or when treated perversely, rather than blame others. Preserved in the heart by the superior man, it bears its richest fruit in serving one’s parents.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Virtue is one of two courses Confucius says can be pursued, spreading over four seas like rushing water.

l: laws, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Laws cannot put themselves into practice alone; ministers need them to fulfill duties, and following ancient kings’ laws prevents error, while inferiors’ disregard for proper order violates penal laws.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Propriety governs officials’ conduct and relations between superiors and inferiors, helping preserve the State. Its richest fruit is ordering and adorning service to parents and obedience to elder brothers. It requires respect and prescribed rules; the superior man examines himself and observes it even when others are unreasonable.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Righteousness is man’s straight path and a principle for superior and great men. It requires superiors to observe laws and officers to serve their prince, urging difficult achievements, setting good before the sovereign, and repressing perversities. It is followed by Shun; those who reject it, deny it, or claim they cannot pursue it depart from the proper path.

l: human relations, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The human relations are perfectly exhibited by the sages.

l: sovereign, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A sovereign has duties and should imitate Yao to discharge them perfectly. Benevolence is essential: it preserves the throne, while severe oppression leads to death and lesser oppression endangers life and weakens the kingdom. Effective government also requires the confidence of those in inferior positions, founded on friends’ trust. The sovereign must rectify faults in his mind, because character determines whether acts are benevolent, righteous, and correct.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Confucius is a person presented through teachings, judgments, and praise. He says there are two courses, virtue and its opposite; instructs his children through a song about clear and muddy water; and rejects ministers who enrich princes lacking benevolent government. He rejects Qiu as his disciple and calls for attack on him, more strongly rejects vehement fighters for their prince, praises Yu, Ji, and Yan Hui for conduct and joy amid distress, and says he made righteous decisions in Chun Qiu.

l: its opposite, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a course [one of two courses that can be pursued] Its opposite is the other course that can be pursued, according to Confucius.

l: oppression, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: oppresses people [when carried to the highest pitch] Oppression carried to the highest pitch causes a ruler to be slain and a kingdom to perish. Even oppression that stops short of the highest pitch places the ruler's life in danger and weakens the kingdom.

l: three dynasties, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Three dynasties gain the throne through benevolence and lose it through lacking benevolence.

l: the throne, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The throne was gained by the three dynasties through benevolence and lost through a lack of benevolence. A sovereign cannot preserve the throne from passing away without benevolence.

l: States, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: States flourish, endure, decay, or perish according to benevolence; lacking it, princes lead States to smite themselves first, then suffer destruction by others.

l: Head of a State, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: preserves rule [when benevolent] A Head of a State who is not benevolent cannot preserve his rule.

l: man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A man responds to failed attachment, rule, or politeness by examining his own benevolence, wisdom, and feeling of respect. He has a correct person, studies to remain in harmony with the ordinances of God, and obtains much happiness. His self-conduct precedes others’ recognition, submission, or contempt: when his person is correct, the whole kingdom turns to him; he must first despise himself before others despise him.

l: wisdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Wisdom means knowing and remaining devoted to serving parents and obeying elder brothers, and is examined when one’s government fails.

l: feeling of respect, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Feeling of respect requires duly honoring elders and testing one’s own response when politeness is not returned.

l: family, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: has_root_in Head [in the person of its Head] The family has the person of its Head as its root.

l: administration of government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Administration of government is not difficult when it avoids offending the great families.

l: great families, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: affect person affected by a State The great families affect the whole State, so whoever they affect will be affected by the whole State.

l: State (any one State), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: affects person affected by a State Any one State affects whoever it affects throughout the whole kingdom.

l: right government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Right government prevails in the kingdom by subordinating princes of little virtue and worth to those of great virtue and worth.

l: bad government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Bad government prevails in a kingdom, causing weaker princes and the weak to submit to the strong.

l: princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Princes are judged by virtue, power, and benevolent government: under right rule lesser princes submit to worthier ones; under bad rule the weak submit to stronger, forming leagues and seeking enrichment.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Qi was the destination to which Yue Zheng traveled.

l: small States, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Small States imitate large States yet shamefully receive their commands, like a scholar ashamed of his master’s commands.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: King Wen, a chief of the West born in Zhou near mount Qi and western wild tribes, nourishes the old and regards people as wounded. Ashamed to receive commands, he practices principles in the Middle Kingdom; his rise draws Bo Yi and Tai Gong, and imitation of him enables States to give laws. He dies in Bi Ying.

l: calamities, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_occasioned_by oneself [when caused by one's own conduct, escape is impossible] Calamities may be sent down by Heaven and can still be escaped. Calamities occasioned by people themselves cannot be escaped or survived.

l: Families, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Families ruin themselves first; then others destroy them, linked to princes who are not benevolent.

l: water of the Cang Lang, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The water of the Cang Lang is clear or muddy; its condition determines whether it washes the strings of a cap or the feet, illustrating different applications from beginning to end.

l: Jie, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Jie loses the people and their hearts, thereby losing the throne; by driving people toward Tang and Wu, Jie aids them.

l: Zhou, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Zhou loses the people and their hearts, driving them to Tang and Wu; by aiding Wu this way, Zhou ultimately loses the throne.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Tang holds fast the Mean, employs talented and virtuous men without regard to origin, and gains support as Jie's actions drive people toward Tang.

l: Wu, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Wu was aided by Zhou, whose actions drove the people toward Wu.

l: the present rulers of the kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The present rulers of the kingdom are warned to love and commit to benevolence, which would bring aid from other princes and draw the people toward them; otherwise, they will remain in sorrow and disgrace, involved in death and ruin.

l: the other princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The other princes aid any ruler who loves benevolence by driving the people toward that ruler.

l: those who do violence to themselves, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Those who do violence to themselves reject propriety and righteousness in conversation, making speech with them impossible.

l: those who throw themselves away, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Those who throw themselves away cannot dwell in benevolence or pursue righteousness, abandon both paths, and are judged impossible to do anything with.

l: the path of righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The path of righteousness is something that those who throw themselves away claim they cannot pursue.

l: duty, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Duty’s path lies in what is near and its work in what is easy, though men seek both remotely and difficultly.

l: men, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Men seek duty in remote, difficult work, while each man is urged to love parents and show due respect to elders.

l: parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Parents are to be loved and sincerely served; such service pleases them and is described as the greatest service, the root of all others.

l: elders, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Elders are to receive due respect from each man.

l: the whole land, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: enjoy tranquillity [if each man would love his parents and show the due respect to his elders] The whole land would enjoy tranquillity if each man loved his parents and showed due respect to his elders.

l: tranquillity, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Tranquillity would be enjoyed by the whole land if each man loved his parents and showed due respect to his elders.

l: those occupying inferior situations, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Those occupying inferior situations can govern people only with sovereign confidence, attained through sincerity and understanding what is good.

l: friends, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Friends trust a person who serves his parents so as to make them pleased. A person who is not trusted by his friends will not obtain the confidence of the sovereign.

l: sincerity, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Sincerity is the way of Heaven, attained through understanding good; complete sincerity moves others, while its absence cannot.

l: man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A man considers sincerity and character; his pupil reveals inner correctness through brightness or dullness.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Bo Yi avoids Zhou and dwells on the northern sea coast, then follows king Wen after hearing of his rise and that the chief of the West nourishes the old.

l: Tai Gong, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Tai Gong avoids Zhou and lives on the eastern sea coast, then hears of king Wen’s rise and follows him, drawn by the chief of the West’s care for the old.

l: government of king Wen, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The government of king Wen is presented as a form of government that, if practiced by any prince, would lead to that prince giving laws to the kingdom within seven years.

l: Qiu, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Qiu serves as chief officer to the head of the Ji family, cannot change his evil ways, and doubles the people’s grain levy; Confucius rejects him as a disciple and calls for attack.

l: Ji family, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The Ji family had a head whom Qiu served as chief officer. Its head is described as practising evil ways.

l: ministers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: enrich princes [under a prince not practising benevolent government] Ministers who enriched a prince who was not practising benevolent government were rejected by Confucius. Ministers who fought vehemently for their prince were viewed as even more deserving of rejection.

l: contentions about territory, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Contentions about territory become grounds for princes’ fighting, causing slaughter until fields are filled with people.

l: territory, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Territory can be the cause of contentions that lead princes or their forces to fight and slaughter men.

l: struggle for a city, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A struggle for a city becomes the ground for princes’ fighting, ending with men slaughtered until the city is filled with them.

l: city, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_filled_with people [through slaughter in a struggle for a city] A city can become the object of a struggle in which men are slaughtered until the city is filled with them.

l: land, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: devours human flesh [through warfare that fills fields and cities with slaughtered people] Land is described as being led to devour human flesh when fighting over territory or cities fills fields and cities with slaughtered men.

l: such a crime, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_not_adequately_punished_by death [death is not enough] Such a crime is the slaughter caused by fighting over territory or cities and is said to deserve more than death as a penalty.

l: punishment, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Those skilful at fighting should suffer the highest punishment. Next should be those who unite princes in leagues against others, followed by those who take in grassy commons and impose cultivation on the people.

l: character, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A man's character can be learned by listening to his words and looking at the pupil of his eye.

l: the respectful, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: does_not_despise people (those referred to as others and men) The respectful do not despise others.

l: the economical, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: does_not_plunder people (those referred to as others and men) The economical do not plunder others.

l: prince, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A prince treats and plunders people with despite, fearing their disobedience; consequently, he is not regarded as respectful or economical.

l: respectfulness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: cannot_be_made_out_of tones of the voice Respectfulness is associated with not despising others. Mencius questions whether it can be made out of tones of the voice and a smiling manner.

l: economy, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: cannot_be_made_out_of smiling manner Economy is associated with not plundering others. Mencius questions whether it can be made out of tones of the voice and a smiling manner.

l: Chun Yu Kun, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Chun Yu Kun asks Mencius about the rule against males and females touching hands. He challenges Mencius by saying that the whole kingdom is drowning and asking why Mencius will not rescue it.

l: the rule, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a general rule [for males and females] The rule is that males and females shall not allow their hands to touch in giving or receiving anything. Mencius describes it as the general rule, subject to a peculiar exigency such as rescuing a drowning sister-in-law.

l: sister-in-law (the man's sister-in-law), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: A woman, the man's sister-in-law, is drowning and must be rescued by hand despite a general rule.

l: rescue, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Rescue differs by need: take a drowning sister-in-law’s hand, but save a drowning kingdom through right principles.

l: right principles, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Right principles are identified by Mencius as the means by which a drowning kingdom must be rescued.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Gong Sun Chou asks why the superior man does not himself teach his son.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The superior man learns deeply by the proper course, preserves benevolence and propriety, loves and respects others, and examines himself when treated perversely. He does not contend with a brute and does not personally teach his son because their relationship forbids it. His life-long anxiety concerns his moral example, not one morning's calamity.

l: son (the superior man's son), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The son receives instruction from his father but may fail to practise it. He can become offended when his father responds with anger or reproving admonitions.

l: teacher (the father), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The teacher, the father, inculcates and proceeds in correct instruction; when lessons are not practised or his son challenges him, he becomes angry and offended.

l: pupil (the son), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_offended_with teacher (the father) [when the teacher becomes angry] The pupil, who is the son, observes that his master teaches what is correct but does not himself proceed in a correct path. This contributes to offense between the pupil and his father.

l: correct instruction, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: leads_to alienation [when expressed as reproofs between father and son] Correct instruction is what the teacher must inculcate. When it is not practised, following it up with anger can produce offense and alienation.

l: alienation, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a inauspicious condition [the most inauspicious] Alienation can arise when father and son exchange reproving admonitions. It is described as especially inauspicious between them.

l: Zengzi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Zengzi nourishes his father, Zeng Xi, with wine and flesh, respectfully asks where leftovers should go, and says some remain. This service exemplifies filial piety and is called nourishing the will.

l: Zeng Xi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a parent [of Zengzi] Zeng Xi is nourished by Zengzi, who provides wine and flesh and respectfully asks about distributing what remains. When Zeng Xi asks whether anything is left, Zengzi says that there is.

l: Zeng Yuan, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Zeng Yuan, Zengzi’s child, nourishes his father with wine and flesh. When leftovers are removed, he does not ask whom to give them to and tells Zengzi that nothing remains when his father asks to bring the food in again.

l: self, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_kept kept [by those able to serve their parents] The self is the object of the greatest charge. The text says that those who do not fail to keep themselves can serve their parents.

l: service of one's parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Service of one’s parents is the greatest service and root of all others, the richest fruit of benevolence. It serves parents, grows when rejoiced in, and when grown cannot be repressed.

l: charge of one's self, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The charge of one's self is the greatest charge and root of all others, enabling service to parents.

l: nourishing the mouth and body, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a practice [represented by Zeng Yuan's conduct] Nourishing the mouth and body is the name given to Zeng Yuan's practice of providing wine and flesh while intending to bring leftovers in again. It contrasts with nourishing the will.

l: nourishing the will, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a practice [represented by Zengzi's conduct] Nourishing the will is the name given to Zengzi's practice of respectfully asking to whom leftover wine and flesh should be given. It concerns serving a parent in the manner described as filial piety.

l: great filial piety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Great filial piety is filial service to parents, exemplified by Zengzi: it nourishes their will, completely fulfills what service requires, brings them delight in goodness, and thereby establishes proper duties throughout the kingdom.

l: great man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The great man rectifies what is wrong in the sovereign’s mind, avoids merely improper or unrighteous propriety and righteousness, speaks and acts rightly without calculated appearances, and retains his child’s-heart.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Righteousness makes a prince’s acts righteous and bears its richest fruit in obeying one’s elder brothers.

l: correctness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Correctness in the prince causes everything to be correct.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is firmly settled [once the ruler is rectified] The kingdom will be firmly settled once the ruler is rectified.

l: Chapter 21, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a chapter Chapter 21 contains a statement by Mencius about unexpected praise and reproach directed at parties seeking to be perfect.

l: praise, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: can_be_unexpected cases Praise can occur in cases where it could not have been expected.

l: reproach, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: occurs_when parties [seeking to be perfect] Reproach can occur when the parties have been seeking to be perfect.

l: men, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Men are described as ready with their tongues when they have not been reproved.

l: readiness with their tongues, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: arises_from reproof [when men have not been reproved] Readiness with their tongues arises simply from men not having been reproved.

l: reproof, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The absence of reproof is presented as the cause of men's readiness with their tongues.

l: men, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: like_to_be teachers [of others] Men are described as liking to be teachers of others.

l: evil, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_a disposition [of men] The evil of men is identified as their liking to be teachers of others.

l: teachers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: teach others Teachers are presented as a role that men like to assume toward others.

l: others, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Others are the people whom men like to teach.

l: Yue Zheng, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Yue Zheng, a disciple who traveled with Zi Ao to Qi, visited Mencius with his lodging-house unarranged and admitted wrongdoing. Though he had learned the doctrine of the ancients, Mencius criticized him for following Zi Ao only for food and drink.

l: Yue Zheng's visit to Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Yue Zheng visits Mencius after arriving in Qi; Mencius questions when and why he came.

l: lodging-house, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_required_before visiting an elder [for a scholar] Yue Zheng's lodging-house had not been arranged when he came to see Mencius.

l: proper lodging arrangements before visiting an elder, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: requires lodging-house [before a scholar visits an elder] Mencius stated that a scholar's lodging-house must be arranged before the scholar visits his elder. Yue Zheng acknowledged that failing to do this was wrong.

l: food and drink, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Food and drink are identified by Mencius as the reason Yue Zheng came in the train of Zi Ao.

l: doctrine of the ancients, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The doctrine of the ancients is something Yue Zheng has learned. Mencius says he did not expect Yue Zheng to act with a view to eating and drinking after learning it.

l: coming here in the train of Zi Ao, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Coming here in the train of Zi Ao is described by Mencius as something Yue Zheng did only because of the food and drink.

l: three unfilial things, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Chapter 26 mentions three unfilial things and identifies having no posterity as the greatest.

l: posterity (Shun's posterity), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: is_greatest_of three unfilial things [when absent] Having no posterity is described as the greatest of the three unfilial things. Shun married because he feared having no posterity.

l: parents (Shun's parents), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Shun married without informing his parents. Superior men consider that action equivalent to informing them.

l: Shun's marriage, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: occurs_without Shun informing his parents [because he might have no posterity] Shun's marriage took place without his informing his parents, because he feared having no posterity.

l: parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Parents are the ones served in the richest fruit of benevolence.

l: obeying one's elder brothers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Obeying elder brothers is the richest fruit of righteousness; rejoicing grows it until it cannot be repressed.

l: elder brothers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Elder brothers are the ones obeyed in the richest fruit of righteousness.

l: music, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: has_richest_fruit rejoicing in those two things Music consists in rejoicing in the service of one's parents and the obeying of one's elder brothers. When they are rejoiced in, they grow, and joy eventually causes the feet to dance and the hands to move.

l: rejoicing in those two things, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Rejoicing in the service of one's parents and the obeying of one's elder brothers causes them to grow. When this rejoicing cannot be repressed, the feet begin to dance and the hands to move unconsciously.

l: Gu Sou, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: finds_delight_in what is good [when brought to it by Shun's complete service] Gu Sou was brought by Shun’s complete service to find delight in what was good. His change transformed the kingdom and established fathers and sons in their respective duties.

l: delight, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: Delight describes the whole kingdom’s joyful submission to an individual and Gu Sou’s enjoyment of what was good. Gu Sou’s delight brought about the transformation of the whole kingdom.

l: Middle Kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The Middle Kingdom is the realm in which Shun and King Wen carried their principles into practice after obtaining what they wished.

l: Chun Qiu, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: The Chun Qiu is a historical work produced after sovereign rule's traces and royal odes ceased. It concerns the affairs of Huan of Qi and Wen of Jin, with Confucius making its righteous decisions.

l: riches, honours, gain, and advancement, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou)
s: are_sought_by men [by various means]

l: Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: This portion of Mencius records dialogues chiefly between Mencius and Wan Zhang, with King Xuan of Qi appearing near the end. It begins with questions about Shun: his filial conduct, marriage, accession, treatment of Xiang, and relation to Gu Sou. Mencius argues that Shun was accepted by Heaven and the people, and that succession rested on Heaven’s ordinance, explaining the different outcomes for Shun, Yu, Yi, and Qi. He then defends accounts of Yi Yin’s counsel to Tang and corrects stories about Confucius’s lodgings and Bai Li Xi’s career, insisting on Bai Li Xi’s wisdom and virtue. The discussion broadens into models of sage conduct, Bo Yi, Yi Yin, Hui of Liu Xia, and Confucius, and rules governing rank, territory, gifts, friendship, office, poverty, marriage, righteousness, and robbery. Finally, Mencius sets standards for scholars’ support and dealings with princes, respectful summons, learning through worthy friends and antiquity, and ministers’ duties to remonstrate, dethrone, or leave when rulers fail.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Mencius is a teacher who instructs interlocutors through replies, examples, and interpretations. He presents filial piety as a supreme human attainment and benevolence as governing treatment of family. He explains Shun’s conduct toward his parents and Xiang, marriage, Heaven’s mandate, succession, and Yi Yin’s service to Tang, grounding Heaven’s will in conduct and popular acceptance. He rejects stories about Confucius and Bai Li Xi, defending Bai Li Xi’s wisdom, talents, and virtue. He interprets the Book of Poetry by its general scope, defines friendship as friendship with virtue without superiority, and sets out principles for rank, gifts, office, poverty, propriety, scholars, support, summons, ministers, remonstrance, dethronement, and leaving a State.

l: Wan Zhang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Wan Zhang is Mencius’s questioner. Across the records, he asks about Shun, Yi Yin, Confucius, Bai Li Xi, and scholars’ dealings with princes. His questions prompt explanations of filial piety, Heaven’s mandate, righteous government, personal conduct, and proper rules for receiving support, meeting rulers, and summons.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Shun is a filial son who assists Yao for twenty-eight years, receives Heaven’s mandate and the people’s approval, and becomes sovereign of the Middle Kingdom. Despite beauty, wealth, honours, and acceptance, he weeps over lacking his parents’ accord. He marries without informing them, and sincerely welcomes Xiang despite Xiang’s attempt to kill him.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Yao, a sovereign, associates Shun in government and presents him to Heaven and the people; both accept Shun after his sacrifices and administration succeed.

l: Gu Sou, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Gu Sou, Shun’s father, did not accord with him; Shun nevertheless honoured and nourished him with the whole kingdom, displaying highest filial piety.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Confucius is a man of Yu, a sage, and a timeous one among sages. He teaches Heaven’s mandate through the people’s perception and hearing, while holding that there cannot be two suns in the sky or two sovereigns over the people; he is also cited on the equal righteousness of forms of succession. He did not obtain succession to the throne because the preceding sovereign had not presented him to Heaven. In office, he follows propriety in entering and righteousness in retiring, treating both office and its absence as ordered by Heaven. He held positions as keeper of stores and in charge of public fields, and responded immediately when summoned on official business. He took office when reception was proper, his doctrines could be practiced, or the State supported him, and departed when they could not. He lived in Wei with Yan Chou You and lodged with Chang while passing through Song in distress.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Tang, a prince seeking Yi Yin, repeatedly sent silk-bearing messengers, gained his counsel, and attacked Xia to save the people.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Yu was presented to Heaven by Shun, succeeded Shun with the people’s support, then presented Yi; after Yu’s death, the people instead followed Qi through natural succession.

l: Yi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Yi was presented to Heaven by Yu but did not receive the throne after Yu’s death. The princes, litigants, and singers followed Qi, Yu’s son, rather than Yi.

l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Yi Yin is a farmer, sage, and servant of sovereigns. First farming in the lands of the prince of Xin, he delighted in the principles of Yao and Shun. Invited three times, he entered Tang’s service to instruct the people and pressed Tang’s attack on Xia to save them. He later placed Tai Jia in Tong until repentance and reform. Taking office in good government and confusion, he accepts charge of the kingdom, instructs slower people, and seeks benefits for all.

l: the sovereign, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: can_present a man [to Heaven but cannot compel Heaven to give him the throne] The sovereign can present a man to Heaven but cannot make Heaven give that man the throne. The sovereign also cannot simply give the throne to another, because Heaven and the people determine acceptance.

l: Son of Heaven, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_a sovereign [of the people] The Son of Heaven appointed an officer to administer Xiang’s state and pay its revenues to him. This prevented Xiang from oppressing the people while allowing him to retain honour and wealth.

l: the people of the kingdom, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: accept Shun [as ruler through their conduct and allegiance] The people accepted Shun after his administration caused them to rest securely. After the deaths of Yao and Shun, they followed Shun and Yu rather than the sons of the preceding sovereigns, while after Yu’s death they followed Qi rather than Yi.

l: the princes of the kingdom, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: attend_court_at Shun [instead of the son of Yao] The princes followed Shun after Yao’s death and Yu after Shun’s death. After Yu’s death, they went to Qi rather than Yi, recognizing Qi as the son of their sovereign.

l: You Bei, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: You Bei was made Xiang’s princedom. Its government and revenues were administered by an officer so that Xiang could not oppress its people.

l: Xia, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Xia was ruled by Jie, whose conduct made natural succession subject to displacement by Heaven. Tang attacked Xia in order to save its people.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: contains the principle of informing parents before marriage [as expressed in its teaching] The Book of Poetry is cited concerning informing parents before marriage, the sovereign’s domain and service, filial thoughts, and the people of Zhou. Mencius warns that its individual terms and sentences must not be interpreted against the general scope.

l: Shun's marriage, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Shun’s marriage took place without informing his parents because doing so would have prevented him from marrying. Mencius says that marriage is the greatest of human relations.

l: Shun's accession to the throne, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_a Heaven's mandate [confirmed by the people and conduct of affairs] Shun’s accession came from Heaven and the people rather than from Yao’s personal power to give away the throne. After Yao’s death, the people, princes, litigants, and singers turned to Shun instead of Yao’s son.

l: Yao's presentation of Shun to Heaven, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: establishes Shun's accession to the throne [through Heaven's and the people's acceptance] Yao presented Shun to Heaven by causing him to preside over sacrifices, which pleased all the spirits. Yao presented him to the people by causing him to administer affairs successfully, so that the people accepted him.

l: Yu's transmission of the throne to Qi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_a natural succession [accepted by the people and princes] After Yu’s death, Yi withdrew from the son of Yu, but the princes, litigants, and singers followed Qi. Mencius says this succession was determined by Heaven and by Qi’s relation to Yu, together with their differing service and virtue.

l: Yi Yin's service to Tang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_based_on the principles of Yao and Shun [rather than knowledge of cookery] Yi Yin entered Tang’s service because he believed that those who first apprehend principles should instruct those who are slower to understand them. He took upon himself responsibility for the kingdom and pressed Tang to attack Xia and save the people.

l: Tang's attack on Xia, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_a righteous undertaking [for saving the people] Tang’s attack on Xia was presented as an effort to destroy Jie’s rule and save the people. Yi Yin urged Tang to undertake this action according to the principles of Yao and Shun.

l: filial piety, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: honours parents [as its greatest attainment] Filial piety is shown by Shun’s lifelong desire for the accord of his parents. Its highest achievement is honouring and nourishing one’s parents with the whole kingdom.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: rejects resentment [between brothers] Benevolence does not store up anger or resentment against a brother. It regards him with affection and love and seeks to make him honourable and rich, as Shun did for Xiang.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Righteousness is a way and inviolable standard governing conduct. It requires adherence to principles prescribed by Yao and Shun, preserving personal purity, and refusing offices, gifts, lodging, or pay obtained contrary to it. It guides judgments about whether gifts and offices are properly received or held, while distinguishing refined judgment from simply calling all wrongful takers robbers. It unfolds through Yi Yin and Confucius, then concludes that righteousness is the way, with propriety as its door.

l: Heaven's mandate, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: determines succession to the throne [without man's causing] Heaven’s mandate is shown through conduct and events rather than spoken instructions. It gives the throne when Heaven and the people accept a person, and it can displace a ruler like Jie or Zhou.

l: succession to the throne, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: occurs_by natural succession [when the preceding sovereign's son is accepted] Succession may occur through Heaven’s choice of a worthy person or through natural succession to a sovereign’s son. Mencius says that both forms can embody the same principle of righteousness, depending on the virtue, service, and acceptance involved.

l: the principles of Yao and Shun, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: The principles of Yao and Shun are the teachings Yi Yin delighted in and used to instruct Tang and the people. They required benevolent government, righteousness, and benefits for the people.

l: Wei, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: contains Confucius [as a place where he was present] Wei was a state in which Confucius lived with Yan Chou You. Confucius was dissatisfied in Wei and left it.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: plans instruction of mankind [through those first informed and those first apprehending principles] Heaven is described as producing people so that those informed earlier instruct those informed later. Heaven's places, offices, and emoluments are mentioned in relation to rulers honoring virtue and talents.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Propriety is a way, with righteousness as the door. It governs giving and receiving gifts, permitting receipt when the gift is properly offered and not gained by robbery. It also regulates scholars’ relations with princes, including support, pay, interviews, summonses, and the conduct required of common men seeking ministers’ roles.

l: office, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Office is sought only in poverty and under low circumstances. It is appropriate when government is good, principles can be practiced, reception is proper, or the state gives support. For scholars, serving while principles are ignored is shameful. Regular officeholders, including gatekeepers and watchmen, may receive princely support; Confucius answered an official summons immediately.

l: Bai Li Xi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Bai Li Xi, a wise and virtuous man of Yu, did not remonstrate when Jin sought passage to attack Guo. He left before Yu’s ruin, became Qin’s chief minister under duke Mu, and made the duke distinguished throughout the kingdom; Mencius denies he sold himself to feed oxen.

l: Jin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Jin borrows passage through Yu with jade and horses, then uses it to attack Guo.

l: the story of Bai Li Xi selling himself, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: The story says that Bai Li Xi sold himself to a cattle-keeper of Jin for the skins of five rams and fed oxen to find an introduction to the duke Mu of Qin. Mencius calls the story an invention by men fond of strange things.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_ruined the ruin of Yu Yu was the state of Bai Li Xi. When Jin sought passage through Yu to attack Guo, Gong Zhi Qi remonstrated against granting the request, while Bai Li Xi did not remonstrate; Bai Li Xi later left Yu after recognizing that its duke could not be remonstrated with.

l: the duke Mu of Qin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: provides a field for action [for Bai Li Xi] The duke Mu of Qin was a ruler whom Bai Li Xi judged to be one with whom he would have a field for action. Bai Li Xi became his minister and made him distinguished throughout the kingdom and worthy of being handed down to future ages.

l: Qin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Qin was the state to which Bai Li Xi went after leaving Yu. In Qin, Bai Li Xi became minister to the duke Mu.

l: talents and virtue, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Talents and virtue concern how a prince should recognize and properly support worthy people. Bai Li Xi exemplifies their value: as chief minister of Qin, he made his prince distinguished and memorable. Extensive information may qualify someone as a teacher, but virtue and talents require appropriate promotion, not improper summons.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Bo Yi, a sage, avoids bad sights and sounds, serves only approved princes, commands only esteemed people, takes office in good government, and retires in confusion; by the North sea during Zhou, his character reforms the corrupt and strengthens the weak.

l: Hui of Liu Xia, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Hui of Liu Xia is a sage whose steady character endures impure princes, low office, dismissal, and poverty without shame, concealment, complaint, or grief. At ease among village people, he carries out principles when employed; his character makes the mean generous and the niggardly liberal.

l: Zhou, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_a House of Zhou [the dynasty whose arrangement is discussed] Zhou established five degrees of rank and six degrees of dignity, with assigned territories and emoluments. Zhou also received from Yin a rule concerning the punishment of robbers.

l: princes, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Princes destroy records of the Zhou arrangement because they consider it injurious to themselves, and are compared to robbers in taking from their people. Yet they may receive properly presented gifts and should assist people, honor worthy scholars, summon appropriately, and heed repeated remonstrance from high ministers.

l: common people, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Common people employed in government offices received emoluments related to what they could earn by tilling fields. Their agricultural support varied according to the class and productivity of husbandmen.

l: sages, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: The sages are represented by Bo Yi as the pure one, Yi Yin as inclined to office, Hui of Liu Xia as accommodating, and Confucius as timeous. Confucius is described as combining these qualities in a complete concert.

l: scholars, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Scholars may accept a prince’s grain as a present to meet necessities, but refuse support or pay without regular office. As common men in city or country, they do not seek a prince’s interview before presenting an introductory present and becoming ministers. Distinguished scholars befriend virtuous scholars; if that is insufficient, they study men of antiquity.

l: the kingdom, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: A scholar whose virtue is most distinguished throughout the kingdom makes friends with all the virtuous scholars of the kingdom. If this is insufficient, the scholar studies and considers the men of antiquity.

l: friendship with virtuous scholars, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Friendship with virtuous scholars is grounded in respect, expressed through presents, and rejects presumptions from age, station, or relatives. It begins with friendship based on virtue, extends to virtuous scholars in one’s village, State, or kingdom, and culminates in studying the poems, books, and histories of antiquity.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_honored_by friendship [as the basis of friendship] Virtue is the proper basis of friendship and is honored by rulers and scholars. Hui of Liu Xia carried out his principles without concealing his virtue.

l: principles, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Principles should be carried into practice by those who hold office. Confucius accepted office when there was a likelihood that his principles would be practiced and left when they were not.

l: poverty, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: motivates office [sometimes, though office is not generally sought for it] Office is not normally sought because of poverty, though poverty can sometimes lead one to seek it. A person who takes office for that reason should choose low status and poverty rather than honor and riches.

l: presents of friendship, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: express respect [as their underlying feeling] Presents of friendship express respect. They should be received when offered on a reasonable ground and according to propriety, but a gift obtained through robbery should not be accepted.

l: respect, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_expressed_by presents of friendship [as their underlying feeling] Respect is the feeling expressed in presents of friendship. Inferiors show respect to superiors through observance due to rank, while superiors show honor to inferiors by recognizing talents and virtue.

l: robbery, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: is_punished_by death [without waiting to give warning] Robbery makes a gift improper even when the donor presents it with a reasonable explanation and proper manner. A robber who kills and takes property is described as deserving death without warning.

l: marriage, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Marriage is generally not entered into for a wife's attendance, though it is sometimes entered into for that reason.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: rules Qi King Xuan of Qi asks Mencius about the office of high ministers. He is initially moved and changes countenance when told that related high ministers may dethrone a prince, but then composes himself and asks about ministers of a different surname.

l: high ministers, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: High ministers are ministers of a prince, divided by kinship to him. All remonstrate over faults; noble relatives may dethrone a prince who repeatedly ignores them, while different-surname ministers leave the State when their rejected advice is not accepted.

l: State, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: A prince who loses his State may properly accept a stated support from another prince. A high minister of a different surname should leave the State when repeated remonstrance fails.

l: support from a prince, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: A scholar may accept a prince's gift of grain or other assistance for necessities but should not accept regular princely pay without an office. Proper support is offered initially with the prince's commission and then continued through the storekeeper and master of the kitchen without repeated direct commissions.

l: remonstrance, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: High ministers should remonstrate with a prince who has faults. Related ministers should do so repeatedly before dethronement becomes proper, while ministers of a different surname should leave the State after repeated unsuccessful remonstrance.

l: dethronement, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Dethronement is presented as the duty of noble high ministers who are relatives of the prince when the prince has great faults and refuses repeated remonstrance.

l: interview with a prince, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang)
s: Common men and scholars without office should not presume to interview a prince without following the proper forms. Even a man of virtue and talents may refuse when the prince summons him in a way that is inappropriate to his character.

l: Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: This unit presents Mencius’s teachings on human nature, moral cultivation, honour, government, and adversity. In debate with Gao and Gong Du, he argues that people tend toward goodness and possess beginnings of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. Circumstance, neglect, and lack of thought can hide this nature, but nourishment, reflection, and steadfast attention recover it; learning is the search for one’s lost mind. He urges people to value Heaven’s nobility, righteousness above life, and what is great over what is small. Mencius then distinguishes true honour, grounded in benevolence and righteousness, from honours conferred by others, and teaches that benevolence must be sufficient, mature, and learned through complete rules. Turning to public life, he treats propriety as responsive to circumstances, connects Yao and Shun’s way to filial and fraternal duty, and insists rulers and ministers reject profit, conquest, unjust taxation, and improper political conduct. He praises love of goodness as fit for governing Lu, explains when superior men accept or leave office, and closes by portraying suffering as preparation for great responsibility, distress as a source of reform, ease as a cause of ruin, and even refusal to teach as instruction.

l: Gao, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Gao is a philosopher who compares man’s nature to qi-willow and water, calling it neither good nor bad. He treats benevolence as internal and righteousness as external; Mencius challenges him, arguing nature tends toward good. Gao also criticizes Xiao Pan as an ode of a little man.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Mencius is a philosopher who teaches that human nature and the human mind are properly inclined to good, with feelings corresponding to benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. Benevolence is man's mind and righteousness his path; learning seeks the lost mind. He explains that adverse circumstances can obscure goodness, but reflection, nourishment, and learning can preserve or recover it. He urges people to mature benevolence and righteousness rather than value honour, wealth, reputation, or fine clothing. In political counsel he rejects profit, weighs propriety by circumstances, criticizes wrongdoing, and values ministers who love what is good. He teaches the ways of Yao and Shun through filial piety and fraternal duty, discusses when superior men should accept or leave office, and holds that hardship prepares people for great responsibilities. Even his refusal to teach may itself be instruction.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Shun, a perfectly filial man, rises from the channelled fields to prominence.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Confucius is a sage and Lu’s chief minister of Justice who leaves after a small offence. The records present teachings on the mind, holding and releasing, universal human faculties and relations, and nature expressed in an ode.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Heaven gives people faculties, relations, and specific laws, establishing a natural basis for cultivating virtue and conferring a nobler human part meant to govern the inferior part. It also prepares someone for great office through suffering, toil, hunger, poverty, and confounded undertakings, which stimulate the mind, harden the nature, and supply incompetencies.

l: man's nature, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Man's nature is the nature of human beings: it naturally tends toward good and includes commiseration, shame and dislike, reverence and respect, and approving and disapproving. It begins with benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge, may be obscured by evil or neglect, and grows with proper nourishment.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Benevolence is a principle arising from commiseration and part of man’s proper nature, not something produced through violence or injury. It subdues its opposite as water subdues fire, though an incomplete amount may fail; its value depends on maturity. It unfolds into a basis for advising rulers and directing government, as superior men lead princes toward benevolence.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Righteousness is a principle arising from shame and dislike, a path people should follow, and part of Heaven’s nobility; when preservation conflicts, it is preferred to life.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Propriety is a principle arising from reverence and respect, furnished in people rather than infused from outside.

l: knowledge, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Knowledge is a principle arising from approving and disapproving, originally endowed in humans and subject to development or neglect.

l: the human mind, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: The human mind has Heaven-given, proper goodness and senses, yet neglect and harmful circumstances can strip or decay it. Learning seeks its recovery: proper nourishment lets goodness grow, while thinking fulfills its office by gaining the right view of things.

l: learning, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: has_as_its_great_end seeking for the lost mind Learning has as its great end seeking the lost mind. It also requires giving the whole mind and bending the will to its subject rather than allowing attention to wander.

l: the nobility of Heaven, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: The nobility of Heaven consists of benevolence, righteousness, self-consecration, fidelity, and unwearied joy; cultivated in antiquity, it contrasts present abandonment for nobility of man.
